title: 5 Leadership Mistakes Limiting Your Influence in the AI Era
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Dempsey addresses educators who want to lead AI-related change but meet silence and resistance. He lists five mistakes: trying to convince rather than building something concrete, assuming title equals influence, equating activity with impact, wishing the system moved faster, and letting salary define worth. Each comes with a corrective drawn from his own trajectory. Build useful artifacts without asking permission, earn credibility through clarity and track record, move from doing things for people to handing over tools, treat institutional slowness as runway, and treat the role as a platform for public work. The thread running through it is that influence comes from artifacts and systems, not arguments or titles. The post leans toward self-promotion and AI tooling, but the leadership argument about influencing up and across without authority is clear.
points: Resistance usually comes from lack of context, comfort or time, so building a low-risk, visible artifact beats arguing for buy-in.
Titles set position, not persuasion; influence in slow institutions comes from giving superiors the map and language to carry change upward.
Moving from done-for-you to do-it-yourself, by building once and extending often, avoids becoming the bottleneck.
Institutional inertia is an opening for those who solve obvious problems with new tools without waiting for permission.
Treating your current role as a runway for public experiments and sharing creates opportunities that a salary alone does not.
quotes: Build without asking. Design something useful, visible, and low-risk. Let it speak for itself. In the AI era, leadership favors builders—not explainers. Influence comes from artifacts, not arguments.
The moment you build something—anything—you collapse ambiguity. You give people something concrete to react to instead of an abstract unknown to dismiss.
Titles define position, not persuasion. They set expectations for managing down, but the real opportunity is in managing up and across.

When you create the path, share the plan, or even offer the language to describe a change—they can take it up the chain. You enable them to lead at their level of influence by guiding them with your clarity.
Busyness doesn’t scale. Support breeds dependence. And if you’re always the bottleneck, you’re not leading—you’re enabling dysfunction.
Most of us think our value lies in doing things for others. That works on an individual level, but at scale, it traps you.
Inertia creates opportunity. Most systems are slow, risk-averse, and five years behind. That’s your runway.
